prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Prince Harry paraded alongside his fellow British servicemen in Scotland Wednesday, as he attended a memorial to service members who have died in Afghanistan. Prince Harry takes part in a memorial parade and service for troops killed during his tour of Afghanistan. Harry, 23, serves in the British Army and spent 10 weeks in Afghanistan earlier this year. He was withdrawn unexpectedly in March after news leaked out about his low-key deployment. The prince appeared in uniform alongside around 200 other sailors, soldiers, marines and airmen at the parade, which took place on Edinburgh's famous Royal Mile. They made their way to St. Giles' Cathedral for a private memorial and thanksgiving service for the fallen service members. Also attending the service was British Defense Secretary Des Browne, families of the fallen troops, and recovering wounded military personnel. Harry holds the rank of cornet, equivalent to a second lieutenant. He was deployed to Afghanistan's Helmand province where he served as a forward air controller. His duties included calling in airstrikes and air support when necessary, guaranteeing the accuracy of bombing on the ground and guarding against incidents of friendly fire. The parade and memorial service took place on the same day Britain's Ministry of Defense announced the deaths of four British soldiers in Afghanistan, and two days after Browne announced Britain will increase its presence in Afghanistan from 7,800 troops to 8,030 by next spring.  Watch Prince Harry at the memorial » . Prince Harry is the younger son of Prince Charles, the heir to the British throne, and the late Princess Diana, who died in a Paris car crash in 1997. Last year, the military ruled he could not be sent to Iraq because publicity about the deployment could put him and his unit at risk. Shortly after the news of the prince's deployment broke, several Islamist Web sites posted messages alerting their "brethren" in Afghanistan to be on the lookout for the royal soldier. Several members of the British royal family saw combat in the past century. Prince Harry's grandfather, Prince Phillip, served aboard warships in World War II; his great-grandfather -- the future King George VI -- took part in the World War I naval battle of Jutland; and Prince Andrew, Prince Harry's uncle, flew Royal Navy helicopters during Britain's 1982 war with Argentina over the Falkland Islands. Prince Harry's brother, Prince William, is also an army officer. But as second in line for the throne, he is specifically barred from combat.

# Prince Harry’s Army years: From Helmand province to royal military remembrance

**London** — Before stepping back from frontline royal duties, Prince Harry built one of the most visible modern military profiles in the British royal family, serving in the British Army for a decade and deploying twice to Afghanistan.

Harry, formally Prince Henry of Wales during his service, entered the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst in 2005 and was commissioned into the Blues and Royals, part of the Household Cavalry. His military career became a defining part of his public identity, linking him to a long royal tradition of service while also exposing him to the realities of modern combat.

## Deployment to Helmand province

Harry’s first operational deployment came in late 2007, when he was sent to **Helmand province, Afghanistan**, one of the most dangerous areas for British forces at the time. Serving as a forward air controller, he helped coordinate air support for troops on the ground.

His presence in Afghanistan was initially kept secret under an agreement with media organizations, intended to protect both the prince and the soldiers serving alongside him. But after the deployment was reported publicly, Harry was withdrawn in early 2008 amid security concerns.

He later returned to Afghanistan in 2012 as an Apache helicopter co-pilot gunner, serving from Camp Bastion. That second deployment lasted about five months and placed him again in one of the central theaters of Britain’s war effort.

Harry has often described his Army years as formative, saying the military gave him structure, purpose and a sense of belonging outside the constraints of royal life.

## Remembrance at St. Giles’ Cathedral

Harry’s military service also connected him closely to ceremonies of remembrance across the United Kingdom, including commemorations held at **St. Giles’ Cathedral in Edinburgh**, a historic church long associated with national mourning, military honor and royal ceremony in Scotland.

The cathedral contains memorials and plaques honoring Scottish regiments and service members, reflecting centuries of military history. Events there have often served as a reminder of the human cost of conflict — the same cost Harry encountered during his deployments and later highlighted through his work with wounded veterans.

For Harry, remembrance has been more than ceremonial. After leaving the Army in 2015, he helped found the **Invictus Games**, an international sporting event for wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans. The project grew directly out of his experience with injured troops returning from Afghanistan.

## A royal family shaped by military service

Harry’s Army career fits into a broader pattern of military involvement within the British royal family.

His father, **King Charles III**, served in the Royal Air Force and Royal Navy. His uncle, **Prince Andrew**, flew helicopters during the Falklands War. His grandfather, **Prince Philip**, served with distinction in the Royal Navy during World War II. Queen Elizabeth II also had wartime experience, joining the Auxiliary Territorial Service during World War II and training as a driver and mechanic.

Even earlier, British monarchs and princes were closely tied to the armed forces, often serving as commanders, patrons or symbolic heads of regiments. That history has made military service a central part of royal identity, reinforcing the monarchy’s connection to national service and sacrifice.

Harry’s own service stood out because it included active combat deployment in a modern war zone. His time in Helmand province, his later veterans’ advocacy and his participation in acts of remembrance helped define his public role long before his departure from official royal duties.
